<!--RsQ_102-->Describe at least 10 behaviours or characteristics that employers do not like to see in job applicants.

generalfeedback.text: Students could list any 10 of the following: poor personal appearance; "know-it-all" attitude; inability to express ideas clearly; lack of knowledge or experience; poor preparation for the interview; lack of interest in the job; lack of career planning or goals; lack of enthusiasm, passive and indifferent demeanour; lack of confidence or poise; insufficient evidence of achievement; failure to participate in extracurricular activities; overemphasis on money; poor scholastic record; unwillingness to start at the bottom; tendency to make excuses; evasive answers; lack of tact; lack of maturity; lack of courtesy; condemnation of past employers; lack of social skills; dislike of schoolwork; lack of vitality; failure to look the interviewer in the eye; limp, weak handshake.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_103-->List and describe the six tasks you need to complete to prepare for a successful job interview.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Do some research. Find out more about the job and the organization. 2. Think ahead about possible questions. Anticipate the questions that you may be asked and practise your answers. Think about questions that you will want to ask the interviewer. 3. Bolster your confidence. Focus on your strengths and positive qualities. 4. Polish your interview style. Practise mock interviews. Pay attention to your nonverbal behaviour; listen to your voice on a tape and work to overcome vocal habits such as repeating "um" or speaking too quickly or too softly. 5. Plan to look good. Wear professional clothing and pay attention to personal grooming. 6. Arrive on time. Be ready when you arrive. Bring your questions, a notebook, your résumé, and perhaps a portfolio of your work.

Vivian is declining the job offer from System Inc.; she considers the interviewer's questions regarding her country of origin and subsequent remarks about her culture, derogatory and discriminatory. The interviewer meant to conduct a stress interview on Vivian and wanted to observe how she handles these queries.

Was the interviewer right in his approach? If Vivian is declining the offer, should she still use the negative messages approach?

generalfeedback.text:
The interviewer is wrong in his approach. He could have asked her questions regarding difficult work scenarios to observe her reaction, but he cannot ask her questions about her country of origin or make derogatory remarks about her culture. This is banned by federal law and she can file a complaint regarding this with the EEOC.
Even though the interviewer was rude to her, she should still follow the negative messages approach: open warmly, state the reasons for refusing the offer, bring to the attention of the organization that their interviewers need to be culture sensitized and be aware of interviewing etiquette, decline the offer explicitly, and close on a pleasant note that expresses gratitude.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_126-->"A single instance of poor etiquette can undo all your hard work in a job search;" therefore, it is advisable to maintain your professional behaviour every step of the way. Narrate a scenario where a seemingly minor lapse of judgment by the applicant resulted in losing out on a job offer.

generalfeedback.text: (Answers may vary.) They could include scenarios involving mistakes committed in the applicant's résumé, attire, interviews, comments (e.g., showing bias), or follow-up communications.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_127-->Which criteria for employees, when used by an organization, would be considered discriminatory according to federal laws? As an interviewer, which of these questions are you allowed to ask and why: "Are you over 18?" and "When did you celebrate your 18th birthday?"

generalfeedback.text: The interviewer is not allowed to discriminate against employees based on race, ethnicity, gender, age, marital status, religion, national origin, or disability. The interviewer can ask if the candidate is over 18, but not questions that can help him or her deduce the candidate's age, for instance, the year the applicant graduated from high school.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_128-->Describe the three stages of a successful employment interview.

generalfeedback.text: 1. The warm-up: This is the most important stage. Interviewers will make important decisions about you based on their first impression. Sell yourself nonverbally. Offer a firm, but gentle handshake; use the interviewer's name; smile. Let the interviewer begin the discussion. 2. The question-and-answer stage: Let the interviewer lead the conversation. Try to tailor your answers to make a favourable impression. Be sure to ask questions of your own about the job and the company. Explain how you will be able to help the company meet its needs. 3. The close: Pay attention to the interviewer's signals that the interview is coming to a close. Thank the interviewer and express your enthusiasm for the job and the organization.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_129-->Describe four ways to respond to unethical or illegal interview questions.

generalfeedback.text: Use any four of the following strategies: 1. If you don't want the job, refuse to answer and state that the question is unethical. 2. If you do want the job, explain that the information is personal; 3. Respond to what you think is the interviewer's real concern; 4. Ask how the question is related to your qualifications; 5. Answer both the question and the concern.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_130-->Discuss when and why you might encounter AI during the recruitment and interview process. Provide one example. How should you interact with AI chatbots during the job search?

generalfeedback.text: You will likely interact with some form of artificial intelligence during your job interviews, beginning with your first contact with a company. To manage the logistics of gathering information and scheduling interviews, many companies now use AI-enabled chatbots to interact with candidates, at least through the initial stages when companies are trying to narrow down hundreds or thousands of applications. These chatbots (which can be either stand-alone apps or integrated into other apps such as Facebook Messenger) typically ask routine screening questions and provide answers you may have about the application process. These bots can make the process more efficient for applicants, too, because they can answer basic questions, handle scheduling, and manage other routine matters without requiring you to wait for a response from company staff. Once candidates move further into the process, various AI tools are being used to screen applicants, administer tests, and perform a first-pass level of job matching. For instance, a system can use machine learning to study the archived résumés of a company's existing workforce and see how their listed qualifications correlate with their on-the-job performance. It will then use those insights to evaluate incoming résumés. You may encounter AI during phone or video interviews as well. Some of these systems attempt to evaluate applicants on a variety of attributes, including openness, humility, and emotional stability. These systems are still evolving and present concerns about reliability and bias, and it's not entirely clear how much value they add to the selection process. However, you should expect to encounter them, particularly for entry-level jobs. The advice for interacting with all these technologies might seem counterintuitive, but the best approach is to act naturally and try to forget that you are interacting with software, not human beings. Stay alert and respectful, the same way you would in any conversation.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_155-->When and how should you follow up after submitting your résumé? How does following up after an interview differ from following up after submitting a résumé?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) When following up after submitting a résumé, maintain professionalism in your communication and adhere to any instructions provided by the employer. Honour close dates and contact the company one week after submitting your résumé.
Following up after an interview also demands professionalism in communication and adherence to employer instructions. A well-worded thank-you message helps reinforce the reasons why you are a good choice for the job. A message of inquiry can be sent two weeks after the interview.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_156-->You received a job offer from Reliable Resources (RR) and you mailed your letter of acceptance within two days, while you were still employed at another organization. Upon receiving your resignation, your manager has a discussion with you and convinces you to stay at your current organization. Since your acceptance to RR constitutes a legally binding contract, would you mail them a resignation letter or a letter declining the job offer, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Though you are in a binding contract, a letter declining the job offer is suitable for this situation because you have just accepted the offer and haven't started working there yet. Moreover, your resignation from your previous organization hasn't been accepted, and you have also decided to stay on at the same company. Under these circumstances, declining the offer is appropriate. Make use of the negative message technique and try to leave the door open for future contact.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_157-->Discuss what blind auditions are in the interview process and why they are important.

generalfeedback.text:
Most people like to think they are unbiased and capable of making fair, objective decisions when it comes to judging or assessing others. Unfortunately, that is far from reality. Decades of research suggests that unconscious or implicit bias is universal and that attitudes and stereotypes affect decision making in ways that people aren't aware of. Even people who consciously go out of their way to avoid biased assumptions can be influenced by unconscious biases that have been accumulating since childhood.
Implicit bias has been a longstanding concern in job interviews and hiring decisions. A case that opened many eyes to the problem involved classical musicians auditioning for symphony orchestras. In the 1970s, women made up only 5 percent of professional symphony musicians. Orchestras gradually moved to blind auditions, where the performer is hidden behind a curtain so the people evaluating them can hear but not see them-meaning they can't make judgments based on gender, age, appearances, or anything other than how well the musicians play. Within a decade, the ratio of women had risen to 25 percent. This concept is now applied across a range of industries and professions.

<!--RsQ_030-->Briefly explain the difference between solicited application letters and unsolicited application letters.

generalfeedback.text: A solicited application letter is written in response to an announced job opening. An unsolicited letter is sent to an organization that has not announced an opening and is similar to prospecting. In a solicited letter, the writer knows exactly what qualifications the organization is seeking and can echo those attributes back in his or her letter. Writing a prospecting letter is more challenging because you don't have the clear target you have with a solicited letter. You will need to do more research to identify the qualities that a company would probably seek for the position you hope to get.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_031-->Explain the function of each phase of an application letter written in the AIDA format.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Getting Attention: The opening paragraph of your application letter has two important jobs to do-clearly stating your reason for writing and giving the recipient a reason to keep reading. 2. Building Interest and Increasing Desire: The middle section of the application letter presents your strongest selling points in terms of their potential benefit to the organization, thereby building interest in you and creating a desire to interview you. 3. Motivating Action: The final paragraph of your application letter has two important functions-to ask the reader for a specific action and to facilitate a reply. In almost all cases, the action you request is an interview.

questiontext.text:
"Nimbus Infotech has consistently appeared as a top info-media firm, based on the research I did for my senior project in communication networking. So imagine my delight when I discovered the opening for a network analyst in your Vancouver headquarters (Position Code: U23-5478). With a major in network communications and a minor in media analysis, my education has been the ideal preparation for the challenges of this position."

  1. This excerpt is the introduction of an application letter. Is this part of a solicited or unsolicited application message?
  2. If you think this is an unsolicited message, draft an introduction for a solicited message-based on the qualifications of the applicant-and vice versa.

generalfeedback.text:
1. This is a solicited message because the applicant is referring to the job announcement in the application letter.
  2. Answers may vary, but the introduction should explain why the applicant is writing in and should maintain the reader's interest in the application by addressing his or her needs.

<!--RsQ_075-->Describe six of the common types of interviews.

generalfeedback.text: (Answers may vary.) 1. Structured interviews-Generally used in the screening stage, these interviews ask a series of prepared questions in a set order. All applicants are asked the same questions, and their answers are compared. 2. Open-ended interviews-Less formal and structured and have a conversational tone. 3. Panel interviews-Applicants meet with several interviewers at once. 4. Group interviews-To judge interpersonal skills, some employers meet with several candidates simultaneously to see how they interact. 5. Behavioural interviews-Applicants are asked to relate specific incidents and experiences from their past. 6. Situational interviews-The questions focus on how an applicant would handle various hypothetical situations on the job. 7. Working interviews-Applicants actually perform a job-related activity during the interview. 8. Stress interviews-These interviews try to put applicants in a difficult or stressful situation and then observe how well they can handle it.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_076-->Describe the three stages in a typical sequence of interviews.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Screening Stage-these usually occur on campus or via phone. They are short; the focus is on screening out unqualified applicants. Try to make yourself memorable while giving short, relevant examples about your experience. 2. Selection Stage-these are onsite interviews with several employees of the organization. This allows the applicant and the organization to decide if they will be a good fit for one another. 3. The Final Stage-this is usually an interview with a higher level executive who can make the final decision and negotiate the terms of an offer.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_077-->Explain what you should expect and focus on during a selection interview.

generalfeedback.text: A selection interview almost always takes place on-site at the company or organization. You will meet with several people-either all at once or sequentially over several hours. Usually, you will meet with a human resources representative, your potential supervisor, and some potential colleagues. They will all be trying to determine if you can do the job and if you would be a good fit with your colleagues. You should briefly discuss all of your strengths, but try to focus on three or four of your best qualifications in some depth. It's also important for you to try to find out as much about the job and the organization's culture as possible. You want to determine whether the job will be a good fit for your goals and abilities. Listen carefully, ask insightful questions, and display enthusiasm.
